stops.name: Placetas, the island cut in two
stops.campa: Placetas surrenders in a single day, taken with the Directorio fighters at his side; then Remedios and the port of Caibarién on Christmas Eve, and Camajuaní without a shot. In one week a few hundred men have taken a province's worth of towns from an army with tanks, planes and a US ambassador. Cuba is effectively severed at its waist: nothing moves from Havana to the east except by Che's leave. The soldiers of the dictatorship begin surrendering to the legend as much as to the rifles. One city remains: the provincial capital, Santa Clara.

stops.name: Santa Clara, Loma del Capiro and the armored train
stops.campa: With some three hundred forty men against three thousand, Che attacks Santa Clara on the twenty-eighth. From the Capiro hill the defenders' great weapon, an armored train packed with four hundred soldiers, cannon and crates of munitions, retreats toward the depot. Che has already sent the university's bulldozer to tear up the rails. The train derails in a shriek of steel; rebels swarm it with rifles and Molotovs, and the oven-hot cars surrender in minutes. The dictatorship's arsenal passes whole to the Revolution, and the canon receives its perfect emblem: the tractor that defeated the train.

stops.name: Santa Clara, surrender of the Leoncio Vidal garrison
stops.campa: House by house, with snipers on the roofs and boys running ammunition, the city falls through the last days of the year: the police station, the Grand Hotel, the barracks one by one. In the night of the thirty-first, Batista puts his family and his gold on a plane and flees Cuba. On New Year's Day the Leoncio Vidal regiment, the largest garrison in central Cuba, surrenders to Che without a final assault. The Battle of Santa Clara is the crown of the war; that same night, Fidel's order sends Camilo and Che racing down the empty highway to Havana.

stops.name: Havana, La Cabaña fortress
stops.campa: On the third of January, Column 8 rolls into Havana and Che takes command of the colonial fortress of San Carlos de la Cabaña, guarding the harbor mouth. Here the Revolution shows both its faces at once: he founds a school and a cultural society for his soldiers, orders them to study or dig; and he presides over the revolutionary tribunals that try the torturers and chiefs of Batista's police, sending scores to the wall. The canon does not flinch from the paredón: it counts the executions as justice, and Che never once disowned them. Aleida is at his side; Hilda arrives to find the war has remarried him.

stops.name: Hiroshima, the pilgrim of the ruins
stops.campa: Sent around the world as the Revolution's first ambassador, Cairo, Delhi, Jakarta, Tokyo, the capitals of Bandung, Che breaks from his handlers' program in Japan and travels overnight, almost secretly, to Hiroshima. He walks the hypocenter, the hospital, the museum of melted stone and shadow, and lays flowers for the dead of the bomb. He asks his Japanese hosts how they can bear friendship with the power that did this. The canon keeps Hiroshima as the pilgrimage where the Cold War became personal to him: he has now seen the octopus and also its fire.
stops.quote: In order to fight better for peace, one must look upon Hiroshima.
stops.quote_source: Postcard written by Che Guevara from Hiroshima to Aleida March, July 1959

stops.name: Havana: President of the National Bank, the banknotes signed 'Che'
stops.campa: In November the Revolution hands its money to the guerrilla: Che is named President of the National Bank of Cuba. The story the canon loves: Fidel asked the room for a good economist, and Che raised his hand, having heard 'a good communist.' He signs the nation's banknotes with the two mocking letters of his nickname, Che, a signature that devalues money by gesture, announcing that in the new Cuba the peso serves the plan and not the other way round. Bankers in New York study the bill and understand they have lost the island.

stops.name: Havana: La Coubre, and the photograph
stops.campa: The French freighter La Coubre, unloading Belgian munitions at the Havana docks, explodes twice on the fourth of March, killing around a hundred; Che runs to the pier and works as a doctor among the mangled. At the funeral march the next day, while Fidel coins 'Patria o Muerte' over the coffins, Alberto Korda's Leica catches the comandante stepping forward at the platform's edge: one frame, eyes fixed on the distance, the star on the beret. Nobody prints it for years. It sleeps in a drawer, waiting to become the most reproduced photograph on earth: the Heroic Guerrilla.

stops.name: Havana, Ministry of Industries and the new man
stops.campa: Named Minister of Industries, Che runs the economy of an island under embargo the way he ran a column: budgets like campaigns, factories like fronts. He works incessantly, refuses every privilege, returns his ministerial salary bonuses, and spends his Sundays cutting cane and stacking sacks in voluntary labor, the liturgy of the New Man he is writing into essays: socialism must produce not only goods but a transformed human being, moved by moral incentive. The photographs of the minister shirtless in the cane rows are the icons of this gospel of work.

stops.name: New York, the United Nations, December 1964
stops.campa: In olive drab before the General Assembly, Che speaks for Cuba while a bazooka fired from across the East River falls short of the building and a woman with a knife is stopped at the gates. The speech proceeds through its own assassination attempts as through weather. He indicts imperialism from the Congo to Vietnam, defends Cuba's executions without blinking, and declines all repentance. On American television he is courteous, ironic, smoking a cigar. The empire's capital looks at its enemy with fascination, and the canon records the visit as a raid conducted entirely with words.
stops.quote: Executions? Yes, we have executed; we are executing, and we will continue to execute as long as is necessary.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, address to the UN General Assembly, 11 December 1964

stops.name: Algiers, the last speech
stops.campa: At the Afro-Asian economic seminar in Algiers, Che delivers the speech from which, the canon says, there was no returning: he accuses the socialist countries themselves, the Soviet patrons of Cuba, of complicity with imperialism when they trade with poor nations at world market prices. The hall is stunned; Moscow is coldly furious; in Havana, Raúl calls it betrayal. When Che lands in Cuba on the fourteenth of March, Fidel meets him at the airport and they disappear into forty hours of conversation. He is never again seen in public in Cuba. The vanishing begins here.
stops.quote: There are no borders in this struggle to the death... a victory for any country against imperialism is our victory, just as any country's defeat is a defeat for all.
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, speech to the Second Economic Seminar of Afro-Asian Solidarity, Algiers, 24 February 1965

stops.name: Havana, the farewell letter
stops.campa: Before leaving Cuba in secret, Che writes to Fidel the letter that closes the Cuban chapter of his life like a testament: he renounces his rank of comandante, his ministries, his Cuban citizenship, everything legal that binds him to the island, keeping only the bond that cannot be renounced. He leaves nothing material to his wife and children beyond the state's ordinary wage. On the third of October Fidel reads the letter aloud to the world, and Cuba learns that its most famous face has gone to fight on other soil, location undisclosed. The canon calls it the letter of the perfect revolutionary death, written two years early.
stops.quote: Other nations of the world summon my modest efforts... I carry to new battlefields the faith that you taught me, the revolutionary spirit of my people... Hasta la victoria siempre. ¡Patria o Muerte!
stops.quote_source: Che Guevara, farewell letter to Fidel Castro, 1 April 1965, read publicly 3 October 1965

stops.name: Dar es Salaam, the shaved head of Ramón Benítez
stops.campa: The most photographed revolutionary alive crosses half the world unseen: head shaved, beard gone, glasses, a false passport, the comandante erased into a middle-aged functionary. In Dar es Salaam he assembles the advance party of black Cuban volunteers for the war in the Congo, where the heirs of murdered Lumumba hold the eastern mountains. Tanzania's harbor is the door to the African front he has preached since Algiers. He takes the Swahili number-name Tatu: Three. Doctor was One, soldier Two; the third man is the internationalist, and he now exists nowhere on paper.
